terminal.description: A shell in your workspace where the demo opens Greta's order list and two of her links.

tasks.title: Catch a customer opening someone else's order
tasks.description:
Before you change anything, prove the hole. In `src/reproduce.js`, implement `reproduceOrderPeek()`.

Sign in as one customer, with a session `{ customerId }` and an id from `seed.js`, and ask the original `getOrder()` for an order that belongs to another customer. Use a fresh `openDb()`. Return an object with:

- `session` and `orderId`: what you asked with
- `shown`: exactly what `getOrder(db, session, orderId)` returned

The check runs your function against the original `orders.js`. It passes when `shown` is real and is an order of another customer.
nextSteps: Run `node src/demo.js` and look at Greta's order numbers.
Find in `seed.js` an order that belongs to someone else.
Open it with Greta's session, the way a changed link would.
Run the demo again and read whose address `shown` holds.
hints: The order page takes its number from the link, and a customer can type any number there.
getOrder never looks at the session. Any order number that exists opens, whoever asks.
Use the session { customerId: 102 } and the order number 2041, which is Greta's.

tasks.title: Show an order only to its customer
tasks.description:
Fix `getOrder(db, session, orderId)` in `src/orders.js` so a customer can only ever open their own orders.

- A customer's own order comes back in full, as `{ id, title, status, note, shipTo, total }`, whether `orderId` is a number or the text of a number from a link.
- An order that belongs to someone else gives `null`, exactly like an order that does not exist. It never throws and never says whose it is.
- An order that does not exist gives `null`.

The check opens orders of every customer with every customer's session, and one number with no order.
nextSteps: Read how `listOrders` keeps to one customer.
Decide where `getOrder` should learn who is asking.
Make an order of someone else look exactly like a missing one.
Run `node src/demo.js` and try one of Cosmo's numbers with Greta's session.
hints: The cause is that getOrder only asks whether the order exists, never whose it is. The session knows who is signed in.
The order list is already safe because its query keeps to the session's customer. The single order can ask the database the same question.
Add AND customer_id = ? to the query and pass session.customerId as the second value. A row that is not theirs is then simply not found.

videos.title: Changing a number to reach someone else's data

tasks.title: Write the test that would have caught it
tasks.description:
Write vitest tests in `src/orders.test.js` that guard this hole for good. Use a fresh `openDb()` and sessions such as `{ customerId: 101 }`.

The check runs your test file four times: beside the original `orders.js` (it must fail), beside a correct fix (it must pass), beside a fix that throws an error saying the order belongs to another customer (it must fail) and beside a fix that gives `null` for every order (it must fail).
nextSteps: Open one of Greta's orders with Cosmo's session.
Say exactly what the answer should be, the same as for a number with no order.
hints: A test that only opens a customer's own order passes on the original code. The hole is in what another customer gets.
The fix that throws keeps the order hidden, but it answers differently than for a missing order. Assert the exact answer.
Expect getOrder(db, { customerId: 102 }, 2041) toBeNull(), and keep one test that Greta still opens 2041.
